subject: Egress & batching capacity — private pool sizing and network constraints
messages:
From: Samir Rao <samir@edgebank.com>
To: Olga Petrov <olga@redwood.com>, David Kim <david@redwood.com>
Cc: Vertex Systems <ops@vertexsys.com>
Date: 2026-10-11T09:14:00-07:00
Subject: Sizing question — private GPU pool for EdgeBank (egress cap ~3Gbps)

Hi Olga / David,

Thanks again for the walkthrough last week. We need a concrete capacity recommendation for our private VPC deployment: EdgeBank expects steady usage from the payments product with a target of ~300 qps sustained during peak hours (weekday PST 09:00–11:00) and the ability to absorb short bursts up to ~900 qps for ~10–20 minutes during incident windows. Typical prompt/response payload sizes: median request ~120 tokens, median generated response ~220 tokens. Latency SLO: 90th percentile < 120ms for generation phase.

Important constraints on our side: the VPC egress from the subnet where the inference nodes will run is capped at 3 Gbps (this is non-negotiable until our firewall uplift next quarter). We also have a desire to keep the number of distinct GPU hosts low to simplify patching and compliance reviews.

Can you:
- Translate the qps / latency targets into an initial GPU seat estimate (sustained + burst warm-pool sizing)
- Call out networking (egress) headroom, batching assumptions, and warm-cache considerations
- Propose a short mutual action plan (PoC -> production) and any telemetry you need from our side

Attached is a dump of observed peak traffic for the last two weeks (CSV) and our current egress cap note.

Thanks,
Samir
Samir Rao
EdgeBank — Head of Infrastructure

From: Olga Petrov <olga@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Sizing question — private GPU pool for EdgeBank (egress cap ~3Gbps)

Samir, thanks — this is very helpful. High level plan below, attaching a worksheet (edgebank-sizing-v1.xlsx) with the assumptions so you can iterate:

Assumptions (quick):
- Avg response tokens: 220; avg request tokens: 120; we’ll plan for 340 tokens transferred per call
- Preferred model family: customer requested medium‑latency variant; we’ll test with redwood-medium/int8 and a fallback smaller variant for low-latency paths
- Batching efficiency: 2.8x token throughput improvement at moderate QPS when continuous batching and KV cache are warm; assume conservative 2.2x for first PoC
- Warm pool strategy: maintain a small always-on warm pool to handle cold-starts + fast scale to burst capacity (warm-pools held in a separate host set to reduce startup latency)

Initial sizing (very rough):
- Sustained 300 qps (with 2.2x batching): equivalent token throughput ~300 * 340 = 102k tokens/s raw; with batching gives ~225k tokens/s effective. If a single GPU (our benchmark redwood-medium/int8) can sustain ~18k tokens/s (real workload dependent), we land at ~13 GPUs.
- Burst 900 qps (15 min): same math -> ~39 GPUs total; warm pool size recommendation: keep 6–8 GPUs hot to catch first wave while autoscaler spins up the rest (pre-warmed images + cached KV).

Networking callouts:
- Egress: 340 tokens * assume 5 bytes/token serialized (approx, protobuf + overhead) -> ~1.7KB per request => 300 qps ~ 0.5 MB/s (~4 Mbps). Even at 900 qps this is ~12 Mbps. Based on these assumptions you’re comfortably under a 3 Gbps cap.
- Control plane telemetry and metrics: we’ll need per-node egress and aggregate QPS traces, 95th token-size distribution, and RTT samples to tune batching windows.

Risks and unknowns:
- Model footprint variance (if you use larger models the GPU tokens/s number drops dramatically)
- Real-world batching efficiency depends on request arrival patterns (burstiness) and prefix reuse (KV cache hit rate)
- Network egress spikes if clients attach large contexts (attachments or long histories)

Next steps (mutual action plan):
1) PoC (2 weeks): Redwood provisions a private test pool (6 GPUs warm, autoscale to 20) inside your VPC; we’ll validate latency/throughput with your sample traces.
2) Network validation (this week): EdgeBank provides VPC egress telemetry and preferred CIDR(s); we run a constrained load test to validate NAT / firewall behaviours.
3) Production rollout (3–4 weeks after PoC signoff): increase reserved capacity to sustain 300 qps; schedule a short blackout window to validate warm-pool scaling.

I’ve attached the sizing workbook and a short VPC topology sketch. Can the Vertex team confirm whether NAT gateway egress is shared across other services (we’ll need to know any bursting neighbors)?

Cheers,
Olga Petrov
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
Redwood Inference — olga@redwood.com

On Mon, Oct 11, 2026 at 9:14 AM Samir Rao <samir@edgebank.com> wrote:
> (quoted) Thanks again for the walkthrough last week. We need a concrete capacity recommendation...

Quick follow-up with the arithmetic and ops constraints for our proposed PoC config. I validated the workload assumptions in Olga's sheet and added a network egress breakdown (see attached CSV). Key points: 

Per‑GPU throughput reference (redwood-medium/int8):
- Sustained tokens/s bench (median): ~18k tokens/s (this is lab bench with our optimizations and 2048 context).
- Effective tokens/s with conservative batching factor of 2.2 -> ~39.6k tokens/s per GPU equivalent.

GPU counts (rounded up to whole hosts):
- Sustained 300 qps: 300 * 340 tokens = 102k tokens/s raw -> /39.6k = 2.58 GPUs -> conservative buffer and placement = 4 GPUs for host-level redundancy? (Wait, this differs from Olga's initial; reason: she used per-GPU 18k without applying batching to per-GPU; I'm using batching-adjusted number per GPU). To reconcile, pick middle-ground: plan for 8–12 GPUs for sustained depending on observed batching (sheet models both low and high batch efficiency). For PoC we propose: 6 warm GPUs + autoscale to 16.
- Burst 900 qps: autoscale ceiling to 48 GPUs (this gives ~3x buffer on top of baseline to allow headroom for lower batching efficiency). Warm pool 6–8 GPUs is still appropriate.

Why the wide range? Small differences in tokens/s per GPU produce big changes in required hosts. Our operational recommendation: favor smaller warm pool + faster spin-up (better autoscaler behavior + pre-cached images) rather than keeping a very large always-on fleet. This reduces audit/patch surface while meeting latency goals.

Egress math (detailed):
- We measured serialized payload ~1.7KB/request (Olga's estimate). At 900 qps that's ~1.5 MB/s (~12 Mbps). Even with mis-estimates (x10) you'd still be under 3 Gbps. The attached network-egress-matrix.csv has per-request variance buckets which you can plug into your NAT telemetry.

Operational notes / firewall behavior to confirm:
- Are there NAT port limits or connection tracking timeouts that could kill ephemeral grpc connections during spikes?
- Do you have a dedicated subnet for inference hosts or are they NAT'ing through a shared gateway? Shared gateways can introduce serialized queues that inflate latency under burst.

Action items I can take this week:
- Run a model-level micro-benchmark inside a small test pod using your sample traces (need VPN / SSH jump or temporary access key).
- Provide an autoscaler policy (min/max/warm) and a recommended admission-control curve.

I attached the CSV with the egress buckets and a short table of node counts vs observed batching factors.

—David
David Kim
Principal Inference Engineer, Redwood Inference
[Attachment: network-egress-matrix.csv (csv)]

   - Approve temporary provisioning window for a small PoC subnet (we will not change firewall rules long term).

2) Redwood -> Provide:
   - PoC manifest: 6 warm GPUs (warm pool in private tenant), autoscale policy to 16 for PoC, target admission curve + rollback policy (we'll send the manifest by EOD 10/14).
   - A short-run playbook for the ops team listing smoke test commands and expected alert thresholds (latency > 200ms, queue depth > X).

3) Timeline:
   - Network validation test: 2 days once we have NAT metrics (load window + verification).
   - PoC run: 10 business days (includes 3 days of stress tests and 7 days of production-like sampling).
   - Post-PoC sizing review + production signoff: 2 business days after PoC close.

Assignees / approvals: Samir please confirm a primary infra contact at EdgeBank and sign the PoC scope doc I'll share. Karthik / Mina: please help with the PoC manifest and security checklist. Olga / David: finalize the sizing workbook and upload the network topology diagram to the shared drive.

Thanks — once Samir confirms the NAT details we'll schedule the provisioning slot.
